summary: Adds new cipher suites to Transport Layer Security (TLS) that use the Camellia block cipher for encrypting data. This lets TLS clients and servers choose Camellia as an alternative to other bulk ciphers. It is a standards-track document, later replaced by RFC 5932.

eli5.summary: When two computers whisper secrets, they need to agree on a secret code. This memo adds one more code, called Camellia, to the list they can pick from.

questions: what is camellia cipher suites tls
subtitle: Adding a fast block cipher option for encrypting TLS traffic.

tldr.problem: TLS needed more options for bulk encryption algorithms beyond the standard ciphers already defined.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4132 specifies new cipher suites that use Camellia, a 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys, in CBC mode with SHA-1 for authentication.
tldr.outcome: TLS implementations could now choose Camellia as an alternative to other encryption algorithms, offering comparable speed and efficient hardware implementations.

today: RFC 4132 is a Proposed Standard. It was later superseded by RFC 5932, which added more Camellia cipher suites. The base definitions remain valid for TLS implementations that support Camellia.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
RFC 4132 proposes the addition of new cipher suites to the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol to support the Camellia encryption algorithm as a bulk cipher. Camellia is a 128-bit block cipher that supports the same key sizes as the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES): 128, 192, and 256 bits.

Camellia was jointly developed by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric in 2000 and has been extensively evaluated by cryptographic experts worldwide. It was selected as a recommended cipher by the EU NESSIE (New European Schemes for Signatures, Integrity and Encryption) project and included in Japan's CRYPTREC list of approved cryptographic techniques. The cipher is also specified in the TV-Anytime Forum standards for broadcast media protection.
sections.eli5: A Japanese company invented a fast, safe secret code called Camellia. Experts all over the world checked it and said it was good. This RFC says TLS can use it.

sections.title: Camellia Algorithm Properties
sections.content:
Camellia offers significant advantages for cryptographic applications. It maintains a 128-bit block size, the same as AES, and provides three key lengths: 128 bits, 192 bits, and 256 bits. RFC 4132 defines cipher suites for both 128-bit and 256-bit keys, treating these as the most practical and efficient options for the widest range of applications.

A distinguishing feature of Camellia is its suitability for both software and hardware implementations with low power consumption. Compared to AES, Camellia offers at least comparable encryption speed in both software and hardware, while maintaining a particularly small hardware design footprint. This makes it ideal for deployment on everything from low-cost smart cards to high-speed network systems.
sections.eli5: Camellia works just like AES, the most popular code. But it was designed to be extra small and fast on computer chips, especially ones that don't use much power.

sections.title: New Cipher Suite Definitions
sections.content:
RFC 4132 defines 12 new cipher suites using Camellia in cipher block chaining (CBC) mode, combined with SHA-1 for message authentication. These suites vary by key exchange method and key size. For 128-bit Camellia keys, the cipher suites are: TLS_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_DH_DSS_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_DH_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA, TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA, and TLS_DH_anon_WITH_CAMELLIA_128_CBC_SHA.

For 256-bit keys, the same set of key exchange options is available with corresponding cipher suites. Each key exchange method refers to different certificate and authentication approaches already defined in the TLS specification: RSA for direct authentication with RSA certificates, DH_DSS and DH_RSA for Diffie-Hellman key exchange with DSS or RSA certificates, DHE_DSS and DHE_RSA for ephemeral Diffie-Hellman with DSS or RSA signatures, and DH_anon for unauthenticated anonymous key exchange.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds 12 new recipes for how to use Camellia in TLS. Each recipe picks a different way for the two computers to prove who they are and share the secret key.

sections.title: Security Assurance
sections.content:
The RFC asserts that Camellia is cryptographically secure and has withstood extensive cryptanalytic evaluation in multiple open worldwide cryptographic evaluation projects, specifically CRYPTREC and NESSIE. At the time of publication, there were no known weak keys for Camellia. The new cipher suites are believed to be no less secure than the corresponding cipher suites already defined in TLS using other algorithms.

For additional security guidance beyond what applies specifically to Camellia, RFC 4132 defers to the security considerations of the existing TLS cipher suites and the AES cipher suites defined in RFC 3268. This maintains consistency with the security properties expected of well-vetted cryptographic protocols.
sections.eli5: Camellia passed all the tests that smart people use to break codes. It has no known weak spots, so it is as safe as other codes already in TLS.
